title: Typography as a System
summary: This lesson outlines seven critical decisions for building a professional typography system, focusing on hierarchy, readability, and technical implementation. It demonstrates how to move from arbitrary choices to a structured system using specific ratios, weights, and spacing rules.

transcript.text: Typography is a system. Same font, seven decisions between product and form.
Five sizes max. One ratio, 1.25, never hand-picked pixels. 11 sizes collapsed to five.
Three text colors do more than 10 sizes. Primary, secondary, muted. Color ranks inside a line, size ranks between blocks.
Two weights do all the work. 400 and 600. When everything is bold, nothing is. Regular for reading, semi-bold for scanning.
Line height moves opposite to size. 1.1 on headings, 1.5 on body. The same value everywhere is the AI-made tell.
Letter spacing tightens above 24 pixels. -2%. Small uppercase labels open up instead. +5%.
Body text stays between 45 and 75 characters per line. A paragraph stretched across 1400 pixels is unreadable. Cap the measure, not the container.
Numbers in tables, prices, and timers use tabular figures. One CSS property: tabular-nums. Otherwise, the column wobbles on every update.

Seven decisions. One font that reads like a product. Now make Claude Code think like a senior UX designer. UX Engine designs a screen before coding, audits what is broken, reviews the diff, and kills the AI look. Link in bio.

on_screen_text: Cap the measure, not the box.
Think like a senior UX designer.
design_principles: Use a 1.25 ratio for type scales
Use 3 text colors (primary, secondary, muted) for hierarchy
Use 2 weights (400 for reading, 600 for scanning)
Inverse leading: tighter for headings, looser for body
Adjust tracking: tighter for large text, looser for small caps
Limit measure to 45-75 characters per line
Use tabular-nums for numeric data in tables
before_after: A complex, unorganized typography set is refined into a strict system of 5 sizes, 3 colors, and 2 weights, improving readability and visual hierarchy.
